ABSTRACT
Objective evaluation of quantitative imaging (QI) methods with patient data is highly desirable, but is hindered
by the lack or unreliability of an available gold standard. To address this issue, techniques that can evaluate QI
methods without access to a gold standard are being actively dev

summary.text: End of the title, authors (Ziping Liu, Zekun Li, Joyce C. Mhlanga, Barry A. Siegel and Abhinav K. Jha, Washington University) and abstract. Techniques that evaluate quantitative imaging (QI) methods without a gold standard assume measured values are linear in the true value with Gaussian noise that is independent between methods, yet the noise arises from measuring the same value and can be correlated. The authors propose a no-gold-standard evaluation (NGSE) technique that models the noise as multivariate Gaussian with a covariance matrix, estimate the parameters by maximum likelihood without the true values, and rank methods by noise-to-slope ratio (NSR). In numerical experiments it ranked the methods correctly in 83% of 160 trials and identified the most precise method in about 97%. The block is headed "METHODS" but holds only this opening.

blocks.title: INTRODUCTION
blocks.content:
Medical imaging provides a mechanism to study in vivo physiological properties of the human body, and thus
plays an important role in the diagnosis, prognosis, and assessment of treatment response of diﬀerent diseases. To
facilitate decision-making in clinical practice, quantitative imaging (QI), i.e., the extraction of numerical or sta-
tistical features from medical images, is being actively investigated.1, 2 QI has demonstrated substantial promise
in multiple clinical applications. These include the quantiﬁcation of metabolic tumor volume from oncological
positron emission tomography (PET)

summary.text: Introduction. QI examples include metabolic tumour volume from oncological PET, dopamine-transporter uptake from SPECT for Parkinson disease, and regional uptake for radionuclide-therapy dosimetry. Simulations and phantoms provide true values, but evaluation on patient data needs gold standards that are expensive or unreliable. The regression-without-truth (RWT) technique assumes a linear relationship with slope, bias and Gaussian noise, estimates these by maximum likelihood without truth, and ranks methods by precision; it and a later NGSE technique were applied to diffusion-MRI ADC, cardiac cine MRI ejection fraction, SPECT reconstruction and PET segmentation. All of them assume noise independent between methods, which the authors argue is often violated, so they propose a technique that accounts for correlated noise.

blocks.title: Theory
blocks.content:
2. METHODS
2.1 Theory
Consider a clinical scenario where a total of P patients are being scanned by an imaging system. From the
acquired data of each patient, a set of K QI methods are used to measure certain quantitative values. Such
quantitative values can be the mean activity concentration within diﬀerent organs of interest. Our objective is
to estimate the parameters that can describe the relationship between the true and measured values, without
access to a gold standard. These estimated parameters can then be used to rank the QI methods.
We assume that there exists a linear stochastic re

summary.text: Section 2.1, theory. P patients are measured by K QI methods; method k's measurement of patient p is u_k a_p + v_k plus noise, with the noise across methods modelled as zero-mean multivariate Gaussian N(0, C), whose diagonal holds each method's noise variance σ_k² and whose off-diagonal entries σ_k,k′ hold covariances (Eq. 1). True values are assumed drawn from a four-parameter beta distribution with parameters Ω, which keeps them in a range and allows varied shapes. Θ, C and Ω are estimated by maximizing the probability of all measurements (Eq. 2), which needs no true values, using a constrained interior-point optimizer. Each method's NSR is σ̂_k/û_k (Eq. 3); lower means more precise.

blocks.title: Evaluating the NGSE technique using numerical experiments
blocks.content:
We evaluated the performance of the NGSE technique using multiple numerical experiments. In each experiment,
P = 200 true values were sampled from a known FPBD. From these true values, noisy measured values were
generated for K = 3 hypothetical QI methods. Each method yielded outputs that were linearly related to the
true values by a slope of uk and bias of vk. The variance of the noise of each method was characterized by
the diagonal elements of the covariance matrix C. Additionally, the covariance of the noise between diﬀerent
methods were characterized by the oﬀ-diagonal elements of C. Thes

summary.text: Section 2.2, numerical experiments. Each experiment draws P = 200 true values from a four-parameter beta distribution and generates measurements for K = 3 methods with slopes {1.1, 0.9, 1.05}, biases {0.1, 0.2, 0.3} and noise variances {0.04, 0.09, 0.2025}. Two noise-covariance settings are tested: lower, {σ1,2, σ1,3, σ2,3} = {0.004, 0.008, 0.012}, and higher, {0.015, 0.02, 0.03}. With 4 beta-distribution settings, 2 covariance settings and 20 noise realizations, there are 160 trials, each ranked by estimated NSR.

blocks.content:

or a diﬀerent noise realization of the synthetic measurements given the true values. We observe that the NGSE
technique reliably estimated the slope, no

summary.text: Results, with the text layers of Tables 1 and 2. With lower correlated noise (80 trials) the technique estimated slopes, noise standard deviations and NSR close to the true values (true NSR 0.18, 0.33, 0.43; estimated 0.16 ± 0.08, 0.35 ± 0.09, 0.42 ± 0.07), ranked the methods correctly in 78% of trials, and identified method 1 as most precise in 97%. With higher correlated noise (80 trials), estimates were again close (estimated NSR 0.15 ± 0.08, 0.34 ± 0.08, 0.42 ± 0.07), ranking was correct in 87%, and method 1 was identified in 97% of what the text prints as "1, 600 trials", where 80 appears to be meant.

blocks.title: Discussion and Conclusion
blocks.content:
For clinical translation of QI, there is an important need for techniques that can objectively evaluate QI methods
with patient data. In this context, existing statistical techniques assume that the noise between measurements
obtained using diﬀerent methods is independent of each other. However, this assumption can often be violated
since the noise arises in the process of measuring the same true value. To address this issue, we developed an
NGSE technique that models this correlated noise by a multi-variate Gaussian distribution.
Our results from the numerical experiments (Tables 1 and 2) sho

summary.text: Discussion and conclusion. Over all 160 trials the technique ranked the methods correctly in 83% and found the most precise method in 97%, in controlled settings where linearity held by design. The authors want further evaluation on clinical QI methods (reconstruction, post-processing, segmentation, quantification), arguing that common evaluations need ground truth that may be unavailable or not task-relevant: Dice and Hausdorff scores need true segmentations, usually replaced by variable manual ones, and low-dose denoising is scored against normal-dose images that are themselves noisy. Limitations: the linearity assumption, which can be checked partly by testing whether methods' measurements are linear in each other, and the need for many patients, which prior information on the parameters could reduce.
